content.model_answers:
A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is a physical quantity?
 Answer: A physical quantity is a measurable property that can be expressed as a numerical value multiplied by a unit, such
 as 5 m or 2 kg.

 Distinguish accuracy and precision.
 Answer: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the accepted or true value. Precision is how close repeated
 measurements are to one another.

 What is dimensional homogeneity?
 Answer: An equation is dimensionally homogeneous when every term being added and both sides of the equation have the
 same dimensions.

 Name the seven SI base quantities.
 Answer: Length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity. Their
 SI units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain the importance and limitations of dimensional analysis.
 Answer: Dimensional analysis checks whether an equation is dimensionally consistent, helps derive relations between
 physical quantities up to a dimensionless constant, and helps convert units. It cannot determine numerical dimensionless
 constants, distinguish between terms joined by addition or subtraction, or derive functions such as sinθ, exp(x) or log(x).
 Therefore, dimensional agreement is necessary but does not prove an equation is correct.

 Discuss common measurement errors and how they can be reduced.
 Answer: Systematic errors shift readings consistently and may arise from zero error, calibration or the method used; calibrate
 instruments and correct zero errors to reduce them. Random errors vary unpredictably; repeat measurements and use the
 mean. Personal/parallax errors can be reduced by reading scales at eye level. Use suitable instruments, avoid disturbing the
 system, record units and quote uncertainty and significant figures.

chapters.title: Vector

content.overview:
A scalar has magnitude only, whereas a vector has both magnitude and direction. Vectors may be represented by directed line
  segments and resolved into perpendicular components. Vector addition follows the triangle or parallelogram law. The dot product
  produces a scalar and the cross product produces a vector perpendicular to the plane of the two factors.
key_terms: Scalar: quantity with magnitude only, e.g. mass or temperature.
Vector: quantity with magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement or force.

Unit vector: vector of magnitude one used to specify direction.
Resultant: single vector having the same combined effect as a set of vectors.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is a unit vector?
 Answer: A unit vector is a vector whose magnitude is exactly one. It indicates direction and is often written as î, ■ or k■ along
 the coordinate axes.

 State the parallelogram law of vector addition.
 Answer: If two vectors acting at a point are represented by the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is
 represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal through that point.

 Distinguish scalar and vector quantities.
 Answer: A scalar has magnitude only, such as mass, time or temperature. A vector has both magnitude and direction, such
 as displacement, velocity or force.

 When is the dot product of two vectors zero?
 Answer: A·B = AB cosθ is zero when either vector is zero or, for non-zero vectors, when they are perpendicular (θ = 90°).

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain resolution of a vector into rectangular components and show how the resultant of two
 perpendicular vectors is obtained.
 Answer: For a vector A making angle θ with the positive x-axis, its perpendicular components are Ax = A cosθ and Ay = A
 sinθ. Conversely, A = Ax î + Ay ■. For perpendicular vectors P and Q, the resultant magnitude is R = √(P² + Q²), and its
 direction from P is θ = tan■¹(Q/P). The signs of components determine the correct quadrant.

 Compare scalar product and vector product, including their physical applications.
 Answer: The scalar (dot) product is A·B = AB cosθ; its result is a scalar and is commutative. Work W = F·s is an example. The
 vector (cross) product is A×B with magnitude AB sinθ; its direction is perpendicular to both vectors by the right-hand rule and
 it is anti-commutative. Torque τ = r×F and angular momentum L = r×p are examples.

chapters.title: Dynamics

content.overview:
Kinematics describes motion without discussing its causes; dynamics relates motion to forces. Displacement, velocity and acceleration
  are vector quantities. For constant acceleration, the equations of motion connect initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time and
  displacement. Projectile motion combines uniform horizontal motion with vertically accelerated motion. Circular motion requires
  centripetal acceleration directed toward the centre.
key_terms: Displacement: change in position in a specified direction.
Velocity: rate of change of displacement.
Acceleration: rate of change of velocity.
Projectile: object moving under gravity after being projected, neglecting air resistance.
study_notes: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.
For a projectile landing at its launch height: T = 2u sinθ/g; H = u²sin²θ/(2g); R = u²sin2θ/g.
Centripetal acceleration ac = v²/r = ω²r.
The slope of a displacement-time graph gives velocity; the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration.
content.worked_example: A car accelerates uniformly from 5 m s■¹ at 2 m s■² for 4 s. Final velocity = 5 + 2(4) = 13 m s■¹; displacement = 5(4) + ½(2)(16) = 36 m.

content.model_answers:
A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is uniform acceleration?
 Answer: Uniform acceleration is constant acceleration: the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.

 Why is projectile motion two-dimensional?
 Answer: A projectile has independent horizontal and vertical motion. Its horizontal velocity is constant (neglecting air
 resistance), while its vertical velocity changes under gravity, so its path lies in a plane.

 Define centripetal acceleration.
 Answer: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration of an object moving in a circular path, directed towards the centre. Its
 magnitude is ac = v²/r = ω²r.

 What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
 Answer: The signed area under a velocity-time graph over a time interval gives the object's displacement during that interval.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Derive the equations of motion for uniform acceleration using a velocity-time graph.
 Answer: For initial velocity u, final velocity v after time t and constant acceleration a, the graph is a straight line. Its slope gives
 a = (v−u)/t, hence v = u + at. Displacement is the area under the graph: s = average velocity × t = (u+v)t/2. Substituting v =
 u+at gives s = ut + ½at². Eliminating t using v−u = at gives v² = u² + 2as.

 Explain projectile motion and derive expressions for time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range.
 Answer: For projection speed u at angle θ, horizontal and vertical components are u cosθ and u sinθ. With launch and landing
 at the same level and no air resistance, vertical displacement is y = u sinθ·t − ½gt². Setting y = 0 gives non-zero flight time T =
 2u sinθ/g. At the top, vertical velocity is zero, giving H = u²sin²θ/(2g). Horizontal range R = u cosθ·T = u²sin2θ/g.

chapters.title: Newtonian Mechanics

content.overview:
Newton's laws connect force and motion. The first law introduces inertia, the second law relates net force to rate of change of
  momentum, and the third law describes action-reaction pairs. Linear momentum is conserved in an isolated system. Rotational motion
  is described using torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum.
key_terms: Inertia: resistance to a change in state of motion.
Momentum: product of mass and velocity.
Impulse: change in momentum caused by a force acting over time.
Torque: turning effect of a force about an axis.
Moment of inertia: rotational analogue of mass.
study_notes: F = dp/dt; for constant mass, F = ma.
Impulse J = F∆t = ∆p.
Conservation of momentum: total initial momentum = total final momentum in an isolated system.
Torque τ = rF sinθ; rotational equation τ = Iα; angular momentum L = Iω.
Friction: f ≤ µsN before sliding; kinetic friction fk = µkN.
content.worked_example: A 0.15 kg ball changes velocity from +20 m s■¹ to −10 m s■¹. Change in momentum = 0.15(−10−20) = −4.5 kg m s■¹; impulse magnitude = 4.5 N s.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State Newton's first law.
 Answer: A body remains at rest or continues in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a non-zero resultant external
 force. This is the law of inertia.

 Define impulse.
 Answer: Impulse is the product of force and the time interval for which it acts; for a constant force J = F∆t. It equals the
 change in momentum, ∆p, and its SI unit is N s.

 Why do action and reaction forces not cancel each other?
 Answer: They act on two different bodies. Forces cancel only when equal and opposite forces act on the same body in the
 same free-body diagram.

 What is the moment of inertia?
 Answer: Moment of inertia about an axis is I = Σmr² for discrete particles. It measures resistance to angular acceleration and
 depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 State and explain Newton's three laws of motion with suitable examples.
 Answer: First law: without a resultant external force, a body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion; e.g. passengers
 tend to move forward when a bus stops. Second law: resultant force equals rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt, or F =
 ma for constant mass; e.g. a larger force gives a larger acceleration. Third law: every action has an equal and opposite
 reaction acting on another body; e.g. a rocket moves forward as gases are expelled backward.

 Explain conservation of linear momentum and derive it for a two-body interaction.
 Answer: For two interacting bodies in an isolated system, the internal forces are equal and opposite: F12 = −F21. Since F =
 dp/dt, dp1/dt = −dp2/dt, so d(p1+p2)/dt = 0. Thus total momentum is constant: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2. This holds
 when the net external impulse on the system is zero.

content.overview:
Work is done when a force causes displacement. Energy is the capacity to do work. Kinetic energy is associated with motion and

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 When is work done by a force zero?
 Answer: W = Fs cosθ is zero when displacement is zero, force is zero, or the force is perpendicular to displacement (θ = 90°).

 State the work-energy theorem.
 Answer: The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: Wnet = ∆K = ½mv² − ½mu².

 Define power and give its SI unit.
 Answer: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = dW/dt. Its SI unit is the watt (W), equal to one joule per
 second.

 What is a conservative force?
 Answer: A force is conservative if the work it does between two points is independent of the path. Work over a closed path is
 zero; gravity and ideal spring force are examples.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Derive the expression for kinetic energy using the work-energy theorem.
 Answer: For constant net force F = ma, work W = Fs. Using v²−u² = 2as, we have s = (v²−u²)/(2a). Therefore W = ma ×
 (v²−u²)/(2a) = ½mv² − ½mu². The change in kinetic energy is ∆K, so K = ½mv² when the reference is zero speed.

 Explain conservation of mechanical energy for a freely falling body, neglecting air resistance.
 Answer: At height h above the reference level, a body released from rest has total mechanical energy E = mgh. After falling
 distance x, its potential energy is mg(h−x) and, using v² = 2gx, its kinetic energy is ½mv² = mgx. Their sum is mg(h−x)+mgx =
 mgh, constant. Potential energy converts into kinetic energy while total mechanical energy is conserved.

content.overview:
Bangladesh HSC Physics | First & Second Paper                                                                                                           Page 6

  Every pair of masses attracts each other. Newton's law of universal gravitation describes this force. Gravitational field strength is force
  per unit mass, while gravitational potential is potential energy per unit mass. Planetary and satellite motion can be explained by gravity
  providing centripetal force. Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape a body's gravitational field in an ideal model.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State Newton's law of universal gravitation.
 Answer: Any two point masses attract with force F = Gm1m2/r² along the line joining their centres, where r is their separation
 and G is the universal gravitational constant.

 Distinguish G and g.
 Answer: G is the universal gravitational constant, a scalar constant with value about 6.67×10■¹¹ N m² kg■². g is gravitational
 field strength/acceleration due to gravity; it varies with location and is about 9.8 m s■² near Earth's surface.

 What is escape velocity?
 Answer: Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed needed for an object to reach infinitely far away with zero remaining
 speed, neglecting air resistance and other bodies. From a planet's surface ve = √(2GM/R).

 State Kepler's third law.
 Answer: The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit: T² ∝ a³ for bodies
 orbiting the same central mass.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Derive the expression for orbital speed of a satellite around a planet.
 Answer: For a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r, gravitational force supplies centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r. Cancelling
 m and solving gives v = √(GM/r). For an orbit close to a planet's surface, r is approximately its radius R.

 Explain how gravitational acceleration varies with altitude and describe the concept of escape velocity.
 Answer: At altitude h above a planet of radius R, g(h) = GM/(R+h)². Relative to the surface, g(h) = g0[R/(R+h)]², so it
 decreases with altitude. Escape speed follows from energy conservation: ½mve² = GMm/R, hence ve = √(2GM/R) = √(2g0R).
 It is the minimum speed for escape to infinity with zero final speed.

content.overview:
Solids and fluids respond to applied forces through deformation and flow. Elasticity describes the ability of a material to regain its shape
  after the deforming force is removed. Stress is force per unit area and strain is fractional deformation. Surface tension explains the
  behaviour of liquid surfaces, while viscosity describes resistance to flow.
key_terms: Stress: force per unit cross-sectional area.
Strain: ratio of change in dimension to original dimension.
Young's modulus: ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain.
Surface tension: tangential force per unit length at a liquid surface.
Viscosity: internal resistance to relative fluid motion.
study_notes: Hooke's law: stress ∝ strain within the elastic limit.
Young's modulus Y = (F/A)/(∆L/L).

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State Hooke's law.
 Answer: Within the limit of proportionality, stress is directly proportional to strain: stress = modulus × strain.

 Define Young's modulus.
 Answer: Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain, Y = (F/A)/(∆L/L), within the elastic limit. Its SI
 unit is pascal.

 What is surface tension?
 Answer: Surface tension is tangential force per unit length acting at a liquid surface, or equivalently surface energy per unit
 area. Its SI unit is N m■¹.

 Why does a small liquid drop tend to be spherical?
 Answer: Surface tension tends to minimise surface area for a given volume. A sphere has the least surface area for a fixed
 volume, so a free small drop tends to become spherical.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain stress, strain and the three elastic moduli: Young's, bulk and shear modulus.
 Answer: Stress is force per unit area; strain is the fractional deformation and is dimensionless. Young's modulus Y =
 longitudinal stress/longitudinal strain. Bulk modulus K = pressure change/(volume strain), usually K = −∆p/(∆V/V). Shear
 modulus Gs = shear stress/shear strain. These moduli measure resistance to different types of deformation within the elastic
 range.

 Discuss surface tension and derive the excess pressure inside a spherical liquid drop.
 Answer: Surface tension γ acts along the surface and tends to minimise area. For a spherical drop of radius r, imagine
 splitting it into hemispheres. The pressure force is ∆p·πr², while surface tension around the rim provides 2πrγ. Equating gives
 ∆p·πr² = 2πrγ, so excess pressure ∆p = 2γ/r. (A soap bubble has two surfaces, giving 4γ/r.)

content.overview:
Periodic motion repeats itself after equal time intervals. Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a special periodic motion in which
  acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed toward it. A spring-mass system and a simple pendulum at

Period: time for one complete oscillation.
Frequency: number of oscillations per second.
Phase: quantity specifying the state of oscillation.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is simple harmonic motion?
 Answer: Simple harmonic motion is periodic motion in which acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from
 equilibrium and directed towards equilibrium: a = −ω²x.

 Define amplitude and period.
 Answer: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position. Period T is the time taken for one complete
 oscillation.

 Why is the simple-pendulum formula valid only for small angles?
 Answer: The derivation uses sinθ ≈ θ (in radians). This approximation is accurate only for small angular displacement, making
 the restoring force approximately proportional to displacement.

 Where is the speed maximum in SHM?
 Answer: Speed is maximum at the equilibrium position, where displacement is zero and all the oscillator's mechanical energy
 is kinetic.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Derive the time period of a spring-mass system performing SHM.
 Answer: For a mass m attached to a spring of force constant k, Hooke's law gives F = −kx. Newton's second law gives
 m(d²x/dt²) = −kx, or d²x/dt² = −(k/m)x. Comparing with SHM equation a = −ω²x gives ω = √(k/m). Hence T = 2π/ω = 2π√(m/k).

 Explain the energy transformation during one complete oscillation of a simple harmonic oscillator.
 Answer: In ideal SHM, total energy E = ½kA² remains constant. At either extreme, speed is zero and potential energy is
 maximum. At equilibrium, speed and kinetic energy are maximum while potential energy is minimum (zero if measured from
 equilibrium). Between these positions, energy continually transfers between kinetic and potential forms.

content.overview:
A wave transfers energy from one place to another without net transport of matter. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to
  propagation; longitudinal waves oscillate parallel to it. Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a medium. Superposition explains

Frequency: number of cycles per second.
Amplitude: maximum displacement from equilibrium.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is a stationary wave?
 Answer: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude
 travelling in opposite directions. It has fixed nodes and antinodes and no net energy transfer along the medium.

 Define resonance.
 Answer: Resonance occurs when a system is driven by a periodic force at or near its natural frequency, producing a
 large-amplitude response.

 What are coherent sources?
 Answer: Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency and maintain a constant phase difference.

 Distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves.
 Answer: In transverse waves, particle oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; in longitudinal waves,
 oscillations are parallel to it.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain the formation of stationary waves and describe nodes and antinodes.
 Answer: Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose to form a stationary pattern. Destructive interference
 produces nodes, where displacement is always zero. Constructive interference produces antinodes, where amplitude is
 maximum. Adjacent nodes or adjacent antinodes are separated by λ/2.

 Discuss resonance in air columns and derive the allowed frequencies for a pipe closed at one end.
 Answer: A closed pipe has a displacement node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. The allowed lengths
 satisfy L = (2n−1)λ/4, n = 1,2,3… Therefore λn = 4L/(2n−1) and fn = (2n−1)v/(4L). Only odd harmonics occur ideally.
 Resonance occurs when the driving frequency matches one of these natural frequencies.

chapters.title: Ideal Gas and Kinetic Theory of Gases

content.overview:
The ideal-gas model assumes molecules have negligible individual volume and exert no intermolecular forces except during collisions.
  Gas laws describe relationships among pressure, volume and temperature. Kinetic theory explains pressure through molecular
  collisions and relates absolute temperature to average translational kinetic energy.
key_terms: Ideal gas: theoretical gas obeying pV = nRT at all conditions.
Mole: amount containing Avogadro's number of entities.
RMS speed: square root of the mean square molecular speed.
Mean free path: average distance travelled between successive molecular collisions.
study_notes: Ideal gas equation: pV = nRT = NkBT.
Kinetic theory: p = ■ρc²rms.
Average translational kinetic energy per molecule = 3kBT/2.
RMS speed crms = √(3RT/M).
For a monatomic ideal gas, internal energy U = 3nRT/2.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
 Answer: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
 This law establishes the basis for temperature measurement.

 Write the first law using the work-done-by-system convention.
 Answer: ∆U = Q − W, where Q is heat supplied to the system and W is work done by the system.

 What is an adiabatic process?
 Answer: An adiabatic process is one in which no heat enters or leaves the system, so Q = 0.

 Why can no heat engine be 100% efficient?
 Answer: The second law requires some energy to be rejected to a colder reservoir; not all absorbed heat can be converted
 into work in a cyclic heat engine.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain the first law of thermodynamics and apply it to isothermal and adiabatic processes.
 Answer: The first law is energy conservation for a thermodynamic system: ∆U = Q−W when W is work done by the system.
 For an ideal gas in an isothermal process, temperature and internal energy remain constant, so ∆U = 0 and Q = W. For an
 adiabatic process, Q = 0, so ∆U = −W; work done by the gas comes from its internal energy.

 Describe a Carnot engine and derive its efficiency.
 Answer: A reversible Carnot engine operates between hot temperature Th and cold temperature Tc through two isothermal
 and two adiabatic stages. It absorbs Qh, rejects Qc and produces W = Qh−Qc. Its efficiency is η = W/Qh = 1−Qc/Qh. For a
 reversible Carnot cycle, Qc/Qh = Tc/Th (temperatures in kelvin), hence η = 1−Tc/Th. No engine between the same reservoirs
 can be more efficient.

 State Ohm's law.

 A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State the right-hand rule for a straight current-carrying wire.
 Answer: Point the right thumb in the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers show the direction of the magnetic
 field lines around the wire.

 Define magnetic flux.
 Answer: Magnetic flux through a surface is ΦB = ∫B·dA; for a uniform field and flat surface, ΦB = BA cosθ. Its SI unit is weber
 (Wb).

 When is magnetic force on a moving charge maximum?
 Answer: The magnitude F = |q|vB sinθ is maximum when velocity is perpendicular to the magnetic field (θ = 90°).

 What is a solenoid?
 Answer: A solenoid is a long cylindrical coil of many closely wound turns. When current flows, it produces a nearly uniform
 magnetic field inside.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Derive the magnetic field at the centre of a circular current-carrying coil.
 Answer: By the Biot–Savart law, each current element contributes a field at the centre in the same axial direction. Integrating
 around a circular loop of radius R gives B = µ0I/(2R). For N closely wound turns, B = µ0NI/(2R).

 Explain the motion of a charged particle entering a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its velocity.
 Answer: The magnetic Lorentz force F = qvB is always perpendicular to velocity and acts as the centripetal force. Thus |q|vB
 = mv²/r, giving circular motion with radius r = mv/(|q|B). The angular speed is ω = |q|B/m and period T = 2πm/(|q|B). The
 magnetic force changes direction of velocity but does no work, so speed and kinetic energy remain constant.

  A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an electromotive force. Faraday's law gives its magnitude, while Lenz's law gives its
  direction and reflects conservation of energy. Self-induction opposes changes in current. Alternating current changes magnitude and
  direction periodically. In AC circuits, resistance, inductive reactance and capacitive reactance determine impedance and phase.
key_terms: Electromagnetic induction: production of emf by changing magnetic flux linkage.
Inductance: property by which changing current induces emf.
RMS value: effective AC value producing the same heating as a DC value.
Reactance: opposition to AC due to inductance or capacitance.
Resonance: condition where inductive and capacitive reactances are equal.
study_notes: Faraday's law: ε = −N dΦ/dt; negative sign represents Lenz's law.

Vrms = V■/√2 for sinusoidal voltage; Irms = I■/√2.

Alternating Current

 A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State Faraday's law.
 Answer: The induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux linkage: ε = −N dΦB/dt.

 What is Lenz's law?
 Answer: The induced current flows in a direction such that its magnetic effect opposes the change in magnetic flux that
 produces it.

 Define RMS value of AC.
 Answer: The RMS value is the square root of the mean square current or voltage over one cycle. For a sinusoid, Irms = I0/√2
 and Vrms = V0/√2.

 What is series RLC resonance?
 Answer: In a series RLC circuit, resonance occurs when inductive and capacitive reactances are equal, XL = XC. Impedance
 is then minimum (Z = R), and current is maximum.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain electromagnetic induction and show how Lenz's law is consistent with conservation of energy.
 Answer: A changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an emf, ε = −N dΦB/dt. Lenz's law gives the negative sign:
 induced current creates a magnetic effect opposing the flux change. An external agent must therefore do work to change the
 flux; that work becomes electrical energy and possibly heat. If the induced effect aided the change, energy would be
 produced without input, violating conservation of energy.

 Describe a transformer and explain the relationship between voltage and number of turns in an ideal
 transformer.
 Answer: A transformer has primary and secondary coils wound on a common magnetic core. Alternating primary current
 creates changing flux linking both coils. For an ideal transformer, the same flux change per turn induces emf proportional to
 turns: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Ideally, input power equals output power, VpIp = VsIs.

content.overview:
Geometrical optics treats light as rays travelling in straight lines in a uniform medium. Reflection and refraction explain image formation
  at mirrors and lenses. Snell's law relates angles of incidence and refraction. Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from an
  optically denser to a rarer medium above the critical angle. Prisms disperse white light because refractive index depends on
  wavelength.
key_terms: Reflection: return of light into the original medium at a boundary.
Refraction: change in direction due to change in wave speed.
Refractive index: ratio of light speed in vacuum to that in a medium.
Critical angle: incidence angle in denser medium giving a refracted angle of 90°.
Power of a lens: reciprocal of focal length in metres.
study_notes: Bangladesh HSC Physics | First & Second Paper                                                                                                         Page 14
Snell's law: n■sin i = n■sin r; n = c/v.
For denser-to-rarer boundary, sin C = n■/n■.
Thin lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u using Cartesian sign convention.
Magnification m = v/u; lens power P = 1/f.
Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n−1)(1/R■−1/R■).

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 State the laws of reflection.
 Answer: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane; and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

 What is the critical angle?
 Answer: For light travelling from a denser to a rarer medium, the critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium
 for which the refracted ray travels along the boundary (refraction angle 90°).

 State the conditions for total internal reflection.
 Answer: Light must travel from an optically denser to a rarer medium, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical
 angle.

 Define the power of a lens.
 Answer: Lens power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres: P = 1/f. Its SI unit is m■¹, called the dioptre (D).

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain total internal reflection and discuss its applications in optical fibres.
 Answer: When light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and its incidence angle exceeds the critical angle, it is totally
 reflected back into the denser medium. An optical fibre has a high-refractive-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding.
 Light is guided along the core by repeated total internal reflection. Uses include telecommunications, medical endoscopy and
 illumination.

 Describe image formation by a thin convex lens and explain the lens formula and magnification.
 Answer: A convex lens converges parallel rays to its principal focus. Depending on object distance, it can form real inverted
 images (object beyond focal length) or a virtual upright magnified image (object within focal length). With the usual Cartesian
 sign convention, the thin-lens formula is 1/f = 1/v − 1/u, and linear magnification m = image height/object height = v/u (sign
 indicates orientation).

content.overview:
Physical optics explains light using its wave nature. Huygens' principle describes wavefront propagation. Interference results from

Coherent sources: sources with the same frequency and constant phase difference.
Interference: redistribution of intensity due to superposition.
Diffraction: spreading or bending of waves at an aperture or obstacle.
Polarisation: restriction of transverse vibrations to a particular direction.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What are coherent sources?
 Answer: Coherent sources produce waves of the same frequency with a constant phase difference.

 State Huygens' principle.
 Answer: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets spreading forward at the wave speed; the new
 wavefront is the forward envelope of these wavelets.

 What is diffraction?
 Answer: Diffraction is the spreading or bending of waves around obstacles or through apertures, especially when their
 dimensions are comparable to the wavelength.

 Why does polarisation show that light is transverse?
 Answer: Polarisation restricts light's electric-field oscillations to a particular direction perpendicular to propagation.
 Longitudinal waves cannot be polarised in this way, so polarisation demonstrates that light is transverse.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Describe Young's double-slit experiment and derive the expression for fringe width.
 Answer: Two coherent slits separated by d illuminate a screen at distance D, with D much greater than d. At a point a
 distance y from the central axis, path difference is approximately δ = dy/D. Bright fringes occur when δ = nλ, so yn = nλD/d.
 The separation between adjacent bright fringes is β = λD/d, called fringe width.

 Explain single-slit diffraction and distinguish interference from diffraction.
 Answer: For a slit of width a, waves from different parts of the aperture interfere. Dark minima occur when a sinθ = mλ (m =
 1,2,3…). The central maximum is widest and brightest. Interference usually describes superposition from distinct coherent
 sources and gives regularly spaced fringes; diffraction is interference among wavelets from different parts of the same
 aperture or wavefront, with a broad central maximum in single-slit patterns.

chapters.title: Introduction to Modern Physics

content.overview:
Modern physics includes relativity and quantum theory. Special relativity is based on the equivalence of physical laws in inertial frames
  and the invariance of the speed of light in vacuum. Quantum theory explains energy exchange in discrete packets. The photoelectric
  effect supports the photon model of light, while de Broglie's hypothesis assigns wave properties to matter.
key_terms: Photon: quantum of electromagnetic radiation.
Work function: minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a material.
Threshold frequency: minimum frequency for photoelectric emission.
de Broglie wavelength: wavelength associated with a moving particle.
Time dilation and length contraction: relativistic effects measured between frames.
study_notes: Photon energy E = hf = hc/λ; photon momentum p = h/λ.
Einstein photoelectric equation Kmax = hf − φ = eVs.
de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p.
Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²); ∆t = γ∆t■; L = L■/γ.
Mass-energy equivalence E = mc².

Space is Euclidean and speed of light is infinite Answer: B

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is a photon?
 Answer: A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation with energy E = hf and momentum p = h/λ.

 Define work function.
 Answer: The work function φ is the minimum energy required to remove an electron from the surface of a material.

 What is threshold frequency?
 Answer: Threshold frequency f0 is the minimum frequency of incident radiation required to cause photoelectric emission; φ =
 hf0.

 State de Broglie's hypothesis.
 Answer: Every moving material particle has an associated matter wave with wavelength λ = h/p, where p is the particle's
 momentum.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain the photoelectric effect using Einstein's photon theory and derive the photoelectric equation.
 Answer: Light consists of photons, each with energy hf. One photon transfers its energy to one electron; φ is used to escape
 the surface and the remainder becomes maximum kinetic energy. By energy conservation, hf = φ + Kmax, so Kmax = hf−φ =
 eVs. Emission occurs only if f ≥ f0 = φ/h. Increasing intensity increases the number of emitted electrons, while increasing
 frequency raises their maximum kinetic energy.

 Describe time dilation and length contraction in special relativity.
 Answer: For relative speed v, the Lorentz factor is γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²). A moving clock is observed to run slower: ∆t = γ∆t0, where
 ∆t0 is proper time. The length of an object along the direction of motion is observed contracted: L = L0/γ, where L0 is proper
 length measured in the object's rest frame.

content.overview:
Rutherford's scattering experiment established the existence of a small, dense nucleus. Bohr's model explains hydrogen's line
  spectrum using quantised energy levels. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Radioactive decay is spontaneous and follows an
  exponential law. Nuclear binding energy is related to mass defect. Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion combines light nuclei.
key_terms: Atomic number Z: number of protons.
Mass number A: total number of protons and neutrons.
Isotopes: nuclei with the same Z but different A.
Half-life: time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
Binding energy: energy required to separate a nucleus into its nucleons.
study_notes: Hydrogen energy levels En = −13.6/n² eV.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What are isotopes?
 Answer: Isotopes are atoms or nuclei of the same element with the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A,
 because they contain different numbers of neutrons.

 Define half-life.
 Answer: Half-life is the time required for the number of undecayed radioactive nuclei (or activity) in a sample to fall to half its
 initial value.

 What is mass defect?
 Answer: Mass defect is the difference between the sum of the separate masses of the constituent nucleons and the actual
 mass of the bound nucleus. Its equivalent energy is the nuclear binding energy, ∆mc².

 Distinguish nuclear fission and fusion.
 Answer: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, usually releasing neutrons and energy. Fusion is the
 joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy when the products are more tightly bound.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain Bohr's atomic model and how it accounts for the hydrogen spectrum.
 Answer: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy permitted stationary orbits with quantised angular momentum mvr = nh/2π and
 do not radiate while in these orbits. For hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV. Radiation is emitted or absorbed when an electron
 changes levels, with hf = |Ei−Ef|. These discrete energy differences produce the line spectrum of hydrogen.

 Derive the radioactive decay law and obtain the expression for half-life.
 Answer: The rate of decay is proportional to the number N of undecayed nuclei: dN/dt = −λN. Separating and integrating
 gives ln(N/N0) = −λt, hence N = N0e■λt. At half-life, N = N0/2, so 1/2 = e■λT½; therefore T½ = ln2/λ.

A. Short-answer questions — model answers
 What is doping?
 Answer: Doping is the controlled addition of a small amount of impurity to a pure semiconductor to increase and control its
 electrical conductivity.

 Name the majority carriers in n-type material.
 Answer: Electrons are the majority carriers in n-type semiconductor; holes are the minority carriers.

 What is rectification?
 Answer: Rectification is the conversion of alternating current or voltage into unidirectional (pulsating DC) output, commonly
 using diode circuits.

 What is the function of a NOT gate?
 Answer: A NOT gate inverts a binary input: output is 1 when input is 0, and output is 0 when input is 1.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Explain the formation and working of a p-n junction diode in forward and reverse bias.
 Answer: A p-n junction forms when p-type and n-type regions meet. Electrons and holes diffuse across the junction and
 recombine, leaving a depletion region and built-in potential barrier. In forward bias (p to positive, n to negative), the barrier
 and depletion width decrease, allowing substantial current. In reverse bias, the barrier increases and only a small
 minority-carrier leakage current flows until breakdown.

 Describe the working of a transistor as an amplifier and explain the relationship between α and β.
 Answer: In a common-emitter amplifier, a small change in base current controls a much larger collector-current change. With
 suitable biasing, the transistor operates in its active region and the output voltage variation across the collector load is
 amplified. Common-base current gain α = IC/IE and common-emitter gain β = IC/IB. Since IE = IC+IB, α = β/(β+1), or β =
 α/(1−α).

 What is a light-year?
 Answer: A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year, approximately 9.46×10¹■ m. It is a unit of distance,

 What is a supernova?
 Answer: A supernova is an extremely luminous stellar explosion, occurring when certain stars undergo core collapse or a
 thermonuclear disruption.

 Define redshift.
 Answer: Redshift is the increase in the observed wavelength of light relative to its emitted wavelength. For distant galaxies it
 is commonly interpreted as evidence of recession and cosmic expansion.

 What determines the final stage of a star's evolution?
 Answer: The star's initial mass is the main factor. Lower-mass stars typically leave white dwarfs; sufficiently massive cores
 can form neutron stars or black holes.

 B. Long-answer questions — model answers
 Describe the main stages in the life cycle of a star and explain how mass determines its final state.
 Answer: A star forms when a gas-and-dust nebula collapses into a protostar. When core hydrogen fusion begins, it enters the
 main sequence. After core hydrogen is depleted, it expands into a giant or supergiant and undergoes later fusion stages
 depending on mass. A Sun-like star sheds outer layers and leaves a white dwarf. A massive star may undergo core-collapse
 supernova, leaving a neutron star or, for a sufficiently massive remnant, a black hole.

 Explain Hubble's law and discuss the evidence supporting an expanding universe.
 Answer: Hubble's law states that the recession speed of a sufficiently distant galaxy is approximately v = H0d, where H0 is
 the Hubble constant and d is distance. The redshifts of distant galaxies show that space is expanding. Further evidence
 includes the cosmic microwave background radiation and the observed abundance of light elements, which agree with a hot,
 dense early-universe model.

   • Schwarzschild radius rs = 2GM/c².

   • A light-year is a unit of distance, not time.

   • Stellar evolution: nebula → protostar → main sequence → later stages determined by mass.
